steps.summary: Set up an inequality comparing our term to $\frac{1}{n^2}$.
steps.why: The $5$ in the denominator makes our fraction smaller than $\frac{1}{n^2}$ for all $n \ge 1$, which sets us up to use a direct comparison.
steps.hint: Think about a simpler p-series where the constant is removed from the denominator.

common_mistakes.hint: A larger denominator means a smaller fraction.

steps.latex: \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^2} \text{ is a convergent p-series with } p = 2 > 1
steps.plain_latex: \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^2} \text{ is a convergent p-series with } p = 2 > 1
steps.summary: Identify the comparison series as a convergent p-series.
steps.why: Series of the form $\sum \frac{1}{n^p}$ are called p-series and we know they converge whenever $p > 1$.
steps.hint: Recall the convergence rule for p-series based on the exponent of $n$.

common_mistakes.hint: Check where the variable $n$ is located; here it is in the base, not the exponent.

steps.latex: \text{The series converges by the direct comparison test}
steps.plain_latex: The series converges by the direct comparison test
steps.summary: Conclude that the original series converges.
steps.why: Since our terms are smaller than the terms of a convergent series and all terms are positive, our series must also converge.
steps.hint: Apply the direct comparison test conclusion since the larger series converges.

common_mistakes.mistake: Concluding divergence when a smaller series converges.
common_mistakes.hint: Being smaller than a convergent series means you are bounded above by a finite sum.

alternates.label: Limit Comparison Test
alternates.summary: Compare with $\frac{1}{n^2}$ using the limit comparison test instead of direct inequality.
